intro:
These exercises drill the one idea the chapter insists you internalize: the JavaScript host and the WebAssembly module keep separate heaps, and the only thing they share is one linear byte array. Everything richer than a number is encoded and copied across a boundary you design. The warm-ups make you state that two-heaps model precisely; the implementation tasks make you build boundary functions that respect it; the debugging and design tasks make you defend the C-ABI invariants and the cost ladder under pressure.

The through-line is that WebAssembly does not remove the marshalling boundary you knew from other runtimes; it makes the boundary explicit. A copy that used to hide inside a marshaller is now a copy you can see, measure, and design around. Each solution below ties its choice back to ownership (who holds the buffer), borrowing (a &str or &[u8] is copied in and not retained), and the per-crossing cost that decides whether the module is faster than the JavaScript it replaced.

exerciseSolutions.title: State the two-heaps model in your own words
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The JavaScript host owns its own object graph: strings, arrays, and typed objects that live in the JavaScript engine's garbage-collected heap and that the module cannot reach into. The module owns its stack and its own heap, both carved out of a single contiguous region called its linear memory. The host cannot dereference module objects and the module cannot dereference host objects. The only region both sides can touch directly is that linear memory, exposed to JavaScript as one shared byte array. That asymmetry is the whole model: two private heaps with one shared byte buffer wedged between them.

Because the shared region is just bytes, anything that is not already a plain machine number has to be laid out into those bytes on one side and read back out on the other. For build_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String, the two &str arguments are copied from the host's strings into linear memory so the module can borrow them, and the owned String the function returns is copied back out of linear memory into a fresh host-owned string. After the call the module keeps nothing: the input strings were borrowed for the duration of the call, and the host now owns a separate copy of the result.

A u32 result from sum_bytes is different because a number is not a heap value at all. It rides the WebAssembly function-call interface directly as a native i32/i64-shaped value, so there is no allocation in linear memory and no byte copy to encode or decode. The input slice still has to be copied into linear memory to be summed, but the answer travels back as a bare register-width number with zero marshalling.
criteria: States JavaScript holds its own GC heap of objects while the module holds its own stack and heap inside one linear memory.
Identifies the shared linear memory (the exposed byte array) as the only region both sides can touch.
Explains each &str into build_label is copied into linear memory and the returned String is copied back to a host-owned value.
Explains a u32 rides the native call interface directly with no allocation and no copy.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the C ABI crossing in route_score
exerciseSolutions.solution:
In the wasm_cpp_ffi_boundary listing, route_score(route: &str) -> u32 is a safe wrapper whose only job is to forward the string's bytes across the C ABI. What actually crosses the inner seam is route.as_ptr() (a *const u8 to the start of the UTF-8 bytes) and route.len() (the byte count). A Rust &str or &[u8] is a fat pointer of (data pointer, length), and the C ABI has no slice type, so you cannot hand the slice over as one value. You decompose it into a raw pointer plus an explicit length, and the shim rebuilds the slice on the other side with std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len) for the duration of the call only.

The SAFETY comments name three invariants that together make the unsafe blocks sound. First, valid pointer: route.as_ptr() points at route.len() initialized bytes (the shim also defends against the null-with-len-zero case). Second, correct length: the length passed is exactly the number of bytes the pointer is valid for, so from_raw_parts does not fabricate a slice that runs past the allocation. Third, read-only for the call's duration: the shim only reads the bytes while the call is in progress and does not retain the pointer or mutate through it, so the borrow of route stays valid the whole time and is not aliased mutably.

The unsafe surface is deliberately tiny. cpp_route_score is declared in an unsafe extern "C" block and its body uses an unsafe from_raw_parts; route_score wraps the foreign call in an unsafe block. Everything else, including main and any caller, stays in ordinary safe Rust. For the input "/orders", the shim reconstructs a 7-byte slice (the characters /, o, r, d, e, r, s) and returns bytes.len() as u32 * 10, which is 7 * 10 = 70.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Confirms the 7-byte length and the resulting score of 70 for "/orders".
criteria: Notes route.as_ptr() and route.len() cross because the C ABI has no slice type.
Names the valid-pointer, correct-length, and read-only-for-the-call invariants from the SAFETY comments.
Identifies that only the wrapper and the shim are unsafe while the rest stays safe Rust.
Computes 7 bytes times 10 = 70 for "/orders".

exerciseSolutions.title: Add a byte-returning boundary function
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Following the sum_bytes pattern, mask_bytes takes the input as a borrowed &[u8] so the module never takes ownership of the host's buffer; the slice is the copy-in into linear memory, valid only for the call. It returns an owned Vec<u8>, which is the copy-out: the host receives a freshly allocated buffer that it then owns separately from anything the module holds. This mirrors how a real wasm-bindgen export of &[u8] -> Vec<u8> would marshal one copy in and one copy out.

The transform itself is a per-byte XOR with key. Using bytes.iter().map(|&b| b ^ key).collect() reads the borrowed slice without mutating it and builds the owned Vec in a single expression. Nothing aliases or writes through the input pointer, so the borrow stays read-only for the call's duration, exactly the discipline the boundary requires. For [1, 2, 3, 4] with key 1: 1^1=0, 2^1=3, 3^1=2, 4^1=5, giving [0, 3, 2, 5].
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: XORs each borrowed input byte with key and returns a freshly owned buffer.
criteria: Signature is exactly fn mask_bytes(bytes: &[u8], key: u8) -> Vec<u8>.
Each output byte is the input byte XORed with key.
The input slice is only read, never mutated, and no ownership of the caller's buffer is taken.
For [1, 2, 3, 4] with key 1 the result is [0, 3, 2, 5].

exerciseSolutions.title: Batch crossings instead of crossing per element
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The point of batching is that the boundary crossing, not the arithmetic, is the expensive part. Scoring routes one at a time pays one full host-to-module crossing per route: N routes means N crossings, each with its own copy-in and marshalling overhead. route_scores accepts the whole batch as &[&str], so the entire list is handed across once and the loop runs entirely inside the module.

The implementation reuses route_score per element rather than reimplementing the shim call, keeping the single unsafe C-ABI path in one place: routes.iter().map(|r| route_score(r)).collect(). The result is a Vec<u32> aligned by index with the input, so scores[i] corresponds to routes[i]. Compared with calling once per route, this turns N boundary crossings into exactly one. The per-call boundary overhead you remove scales with N; the inner arithmetic (len * 10 per route) is unchanged because it was never the cost.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Scores every route in one batched call by mapping route_score over the slice.
criteria: Signature is exactly fn route_scores(routes: &[&str]) -> Vec<u32>.
Result length equals input length and each entry matches route_score for that route.
Reuses route_score instead of duplicating the unsafe shim call.
States the batch makes one crossing instead of one per route.

exerciseSolutions.title: Fix an unsound boundary wrapper
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is that score_prefix passes the caller-supplied n straight through to cpp_route_score(route.as_ptr(), n) without checking it against route.len(). The C ABI trusts the length you hand it: inside the shim, from_raw_parts(ptr, n) will fabricate a slice of n bytes starting at route's first byte. If n is greater than route.len(), that slice runs past the borrowed string into memory the pointer is not valid for, violating the correct-length invariant and reading out of bounds. The wrapper is the only place that can enforce a bound, because once the pointer and length cross the seam the shim has no way to know the true size of the allocation.

The fix is to clamp the length to the borrowed region before crossing: n.min(route.len()). That guarantees the length never exceeds the bytes the pointer is valid for, so the pointer-plus-length pair always describes a region inside the string. The pointer stays valid (it is still route.as_ptr()), the length is now correct (at most route.len()), and the shim still only reads for the call's duration, so the read-only borrow invariant holds. With the clamp in place the wrapper is sound for any n the caller passes.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Clamps the length with n.min(route.len()) so the pointer/length pair stays in bounds.
criteria: Identifies that n greater than route.len() lets the shim read beyond the borrowed bytes.
Clamps the length to at most route.len() with n.min(route.len()) before the call.
The corrected wrapper passes a pointer and length that always describe a valid read-only region.
A SAFETY comment names the valid-pointer, correct-length, and read-only invariants.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose boundary representations on the cost ladder
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Map each workload to one rung of the number / bytes / struct / resident-handle ladder and justify it by copies per crossing plus any encode/decode cost.

Per-frame brightness scalar: send it as a number. It rides the native call interface for free, with no allocation in linear memory and no copy. Doing this per frame is fine because the cost is zero regardless of frame rate.

Parsed config struct sent once at startup: send it as a serialized struct. A struct crossing costs an encode on one side, a copy of the bytes, and a decode on the other. That encode-plus-decode overhead is real, but it is paid exactly once at startup, so the convenience of a structured representation is worth it and the per-frame path never touches it.

Large image buffer processed every frame: cross it as a byte array, one copy per crossing. There is no encode/decode, just the raw byte copy into (or out of) linear memory. The buffer is large, so even one copy per frame is the dominant cost; you minimize it by reusing the same allocation and copying only when the pixels actually change, and by processing the whole frame in a single crossing rather than per-row.

Parser the host calls thousands of times: keep it resident behind a handle. Instead of copying the parser's state in and out on every call, you construct it once inside the module and return an opaque handle (an integer or a wasm-bindgen object) the host holds. Each subsequent call passes the handle plus only the new input, so per call you pay almost nothing instead of re-marshalling the whole parser. The tradeoff is a managed lifetime: the host must explicitly free or drop the handle, and you own the bookkeeping that the resident state is released.

Where the convenient type loses: encoding the large config struct (or any sizeable structured payload) as JSON and shipping it across on a hot path. JSON adds a serialize on the sending side and a full parse on the receiving side on top of the byte copy. For a struct crossed thousands of times, that encode-plus-decode tax can make the WebAssembly module slower end to end than the plain JavaScript it replaced, even though the arithmetic inside the module is faster. A compact binary layout the host reads directly as a typed array skips the parse entirely and is dramatically cheaper, which is the whole reason the performance discussion is about the boundary and not the math.
criteria: Brightness scalar crosses as a number with no copy; image buffer crosses as a byte array with one copy per crossing.
The parser called thousands of times is kept resident behind a handle to avoid per-call copies, at the cost of a managed lifetime.
Each choice is justified using copies per crossing or encode-plus-decode cost from the ladder.
Names a concrete case (a large struct as JSON on a hot path) where the convenient encoding loses to a compact binary layout.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
label = billing::/ready
sum = 10
score = 70
batch crossings = 1
labSolution.explanation:
Each helper models one boundary contract in plain std Rust so the crossing logic is testable without a browser. build_label takes two borrowed &str values (the copy-in) and returns an owned String (the copy-out), printing billing::/ready. sum_bytes borrows the slice [1, 2, 3, 4], sums it as u32, and returns 1+2+3+4 = 10 as a bare number with no copy. route_score models the pointer-plus-length C-ABI crossing as len * 10, so "/orders" (7 bytes) yields 70.

The only TODO is route_scores. The batched implementation maps route_score over the borrowed &[&str] and collects into a Vec<u32>: routes.iter().map(|route| route_score(route)).collect(). This scores all three routes inside one call rather than crossing the boundary per element, which is exactly the batching point of the chapter.

Because scores is non-empty after the batched call, the final println! takes the else-free branch of the if and prints batch crossings = 1, signaling that the whole batch crossed in a single call. Every line therefore matches the expected output exactly.

reviewAnswers.question: Why does every value richer than a number get copied when it crosses between the JavaScript host and the WebAssembly module?
reviewAnswers.answer: The host and the module keep two separate heaps and cannot dereference each other's objects; the only memory both sides can touch is the module's linear memory, exposed as one shared byte array. Any value that is not already a plain machine number is a heap value, so it must be laid out into those shared bytes on one side and read back out on the other, which is a copy. A number is the exception because it travels directly on the native function-call interface with no allocation, so it needs no encode-and-copy step.

reviewAnswers.question: What role does wasm-bindgen play after a browser-facing crate is compiled as a cdylib?
reviewAnswers.answer: The cdylib crate type tells the linker to produce a single .wasm artifact. wasm-bindgen then post-processes that artifact to emit the JavaScript glue that knows how to lay out each annotated argument into linear memory and read each return value back out. In other words, it generates the marshalling code that turns the raw WebAssembly imports and exports into callable JavaScript functions with the right copy-in and copy-out behavior for strings, arrays, and structs.

reviewAnswers.question: On the cost ladder of boundary representations, how do a number, a byte array, a serialized struct, and a resident handle differ in per-crossing cost?
reviewAnswers.answer: A number rides the native interface for free, with no allocation and no copy. A string or byte array costs one byte copy per crossing. A serialized struct costs an encode plus a copy plus a decode, since it must be flattened to bytes and rebuilt on the far side. A resident handle costs almost nothing per call because the state stays inside the module and only a small handle plus new inputs cross, but it adds a lifetime the host must manage and eventually release.

reviewAnswers.question: How do the outer Rust-to-JavaScript seam and the inner Rust-to-C-shim seam differ in how data and safety are managed?
reviewAnswers.answer: The outer seam is managed by wasm-bindgen's generated glue: it handles the layout and copying of each value, so the data movement and most of the safety are automatic. The inner seam is the raw C ABI, where data crosses as bare pointers and lengths through an unsafe extern block, and you uphold the pointer, length, and borrow-duration invariants by hand with SAFETY comments. They stack but stay distinct, so a fault should be diagnosed at the correct seam rather than confused between the two.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is the WebAssembly performance discussion almost always about the boundary rather than the arithmetic inside the module?
reviewAnswers.answer: Inside the module WebAssembly computes at near-native speed, so the arithmetic is rarely the bottleneck. The cost that actually varies with your design is the boundary: crossing per element instead of batching, copying a large buffer on every call, or encoding a struct as JSON and parsing it back. A design that mishandles those crossings can be slower than the JavaScript it replaced even though its inner math is faster, which is why the boundary is where the performance work lives.
